steps.label: S
steps.reason: Excess methanol/dry HCl can acetalize the aryl ketone, while the aryl acetate and bromohydrin are also potentially reactive under these conditions, so the textbook ketalization does not define a unique major product for this multifunctional substrate.

steps.label: V
steps.reason: Excess methanol/dry HCl can ketalize the aryl ketone, methanolyze the aryl acetate, and promote acid-induced rearrangement of the vicinal diol, so these conditions do not specify a unique major product.

steps.label: R
steps.reason: The ortho phenolic OH can intramolecularly trap the Hg²⁺-activated alkene at its more substituted carbon, favoring five-membered-ring cyclization; the separate benzylic alcohol remains unchanged.

steps.label: R
steps.reason: NaOH-promoted retrocyanation of the cyanohydrin releases cyanide, which dimethyl sulfate traps as acetonitrile, while the more acidic phenol is methylated to the aryl methyl ether.

steps.label: R
steps.reason: Excess NH₃ can react at both the ketone and the secondary allylic chloride, and substitution at the allylic chloride can give direct and rearranged products, so no unique major product follows from the stated conditions.

steps.label: S
steps.reason: Br₂/H₂O is not selective here: the alkene can form a bromohydrin, while the primary amine can undergo N-bromination or oxidation, so the major outcome depends on conditions and reagent equivalents.

steps.label: T
steps.reason: The free β-bromoamine can cyclize by intramolecular displacement to an aziridine while SOCl₂/pyridine activates the benzylic alcohol, so the standard alcohol-to-chloride rule alone does not determine a unique major product for this substrate.

steps.label: V
steps.reason: Cyanide can substitute the allylic chloride by direct SN2 or by SN2′ with double-bond migration, and NaCN/DMSO alone does not establish which regioisomer predominates; the ketone is not converted to a stable cyanohydrin under these conditions.

steps.label: R
steps.reason: The substrate has two competing alcohol sites, including an acid-labile cyanohydrin that can cleave under HBF₄, so the standard CH₂N₂/HBF₄ transformation cannot be assigned a single major product.

events.system:
P = 1-[4-(3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl)phenyl]ethan-1-one
P --[CH₃COCl, pyridine]--> Q
Q --[Br₂, H₂O]--> R
R --[NaCN, DMSO]--> S
Q --[Ph₃P=CH₂]--> T
R --[NH₂OH·HCl, pyridine]--> U
events.hidden_link: Students must identify the acylation of the alcohol to form Q, the regioselective bromohydrin formation at R (OH at benzylic position), SN2 substitution by cyanide at S, Wittig reaction at T, and oxime formation at U.
events.route:
1. P has a secondary alcohol and a methyl ketone. CH3COCl/pyridine selectively acylates the alcohol to give ester Q. 
2. Br2/H2O reacts with the alkene in Q. The bromonium ion is opened by water at the more stable benzylic position, placing the OH benzylic and Br on the adjacent carbon (R). 
3. NaCN in DMSO performs an SN2 displacement of the secondary bromide in R to give a nitrile S. 
4. Ph3P=CH2 (Wittig) converts the methyl ketone in Q to an alkene T. 
5. NH2OH condenses with the ketone in R to form oxime U.
events.student_must_notice: The regioselectivity of the bromohydrin formation (step R) yields a benzylic alcohol, which reacts immediately in the Lucas test. Furthermore, NaCN yields a nitrile, not an isocyanide (step S).
events.trap: If the bromohydrin regiochemistry is reversed, R would be a secondary alcohol (Lucas test in 5 mins). If AgCN rules are mistakenly applied to NaCN, S would be an isocyanide.

members.working:
1. Identify P: 1-[4-(3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl)phenyl]ethan-1-one. Structure: phenyl ring with substituent at para position: 3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl (CH2-CH=CH-OH attached at CH=). Ethan-1-one means acetyl group at position 1 of the side chain? Actually overall: the compound has a ketone (ethan-1-one) attached to phenyl at position 1? The name suggests the phenyl ring bears a substituent at para (4-position) of the side chain 3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl, and the whole side chain includes the ketone? Let's parse: 1-[4-(3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl)phenyl]ethan-1-one means phenyl group with substituent at para (4) of the side chain? The side chain is 3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl attached to phenyl at its 1-position? The ketone is ethan-1-one attached to the phenyl at position 1? Likely the side chain is CH2-CO-Ph? Actually typical: 1-(4-(3-hydroxybut-1-en-1-yl)phenyl)ethanone: phenyl attached to carbonyl carbon (ethanone) and also to side chain via para? Might be: Ph-CH2-CO-CH2-CH=CH-OH? Let's assume P has a double bond (but-1-enyl) and a primary alcohol at the terminal carbon of side chain (3-hydroxy). So P has a double bond and an alcohol.
2. Q: treatment with CH3COCl, pyridine = acetylation of the alcohol OH to acetate (protect). So Q is P with OH -> OAc.
3. R: Q + Br2, H2O -> bromination of the double bond (addition) giving vicinal dibromide (or bromohydrin?). Likely addition across double bond, giving a bromo alcohol? Since water present, may give bromohydrin (bromo + OH). But Q already has acetate, no OH at that position? The side chain has OH at carbon 3 (terminal). After acetylation, OH becomes OAc, not free OH. So double bond remains. Bromination adds Br across double bond, giving dibromide (or bromohydrin if water adds). Likely dibromide (cis/trans). So R has a dibromide at the double bond location.
4. S: R + NaCN, DMSO -> substitution of bromide with CN (SN2) at the carbon bearing Br adjacent to carbonyl? Likely cyanide replaces one Br giving nitrile. So S contains nitrile functional group. True.
5. T: Q + Ph3P=CH2 (allylation) -> addition of methylene across carbonyl? Ph3P=CH2 adds to ketone forming alkylidene? Likely forms a new carbon-carbon bond at the carbonyl, giving an enol ether? Might give a new double bond adjacent to carbonyl, producing a compound with a new CH2 group attached to carbonyl carbon, forming a β-hydroxy? But typical use of Ph3P=CH2 (ylide) adds to carbonyl to give β-alkylated product (aldol-type). So T likely has a new carbon adjacent to carbonyl, possibly giving a CH2-CO-Ph side chain with new substituent. This could give iodoform test if it has CH3-CO- group. Q has ethanone (COCH3?) Actually ethan-1-one is CH3-CO-? Ethan-1-one is acetone? Ethan-1-one = CH3-CO-? Yes ethanone = acetone (propan-2-one). But with side chain attached at phenyl? Might be CH3-CO-Ph? Let's assume Q has a methyl ketone (COCH3) at the phenyl side? The name suggests ethan-1-one attached to phenyl at position 1 of side chain? Might be CH3-CO- attached to phenyl? So T after allylation may still have CH3-CO- group, giving iodoform positive. So (3) likely true.
6. U: R + NH2OH·HCl, pyridine -> hydroxylamine forms oxime from aldehyde/ketone? R has dibromide, no carbonyl? But R still has carbonyl (ketone) unchanged. Hydroxylamine reacts with carbonyl to form oxime. So U contains oxime, not aldehyde/ketone, so 2,4-DNP test (which detects aldehydes/ketones) would be negative. So (6) false.
7. Evaluate statements:
(1) R produces immediate turbidity with Lucas reagent (HCl/ZnCl2) at RT: Lucas reagent reacts with secondary alcohols to give turbidity (precipitate) quickly. R after bromination likely has no free alcohol (the OH was acetylated in Q and then bromination may not regenerate OH). So no secondary alcohol, false.
(2) S contains nitrile: true.
(3) T gives positive iodoform test: likely true if T has CH3-CO- group.
(4) Q decolourises bromine water: Q has a double bond (since acetylation does not affect double bond), bromine water reacts with alkenes causing decolourisation (addition). So true.
(5) Total number of sp-hybridised carbon atoms in S is 1: S has nitrile carbon (sp) and possibly other sp? The side chain after substitution may have sp2? The nitrile carbon is sp, others sp3. So only one sp carbon, true.
(6) U gives positive 2,4-DNP test: false.
Thus correct statements: (2),(3),(4),(5) = 4 statements. (1) false, (6) false. So answer integer 4.
